title: Making Choices (If/Else)
story: You're deciding what to wear. If it's cold, wear a jacket. Otherwise, wear a t-shirt. Your program can make the same kind of choice — look at a condition and decide which path to take.
why: Programs that always do the same thing are boring. With `if` and `else`, your code can look at the world around it and react differently. Every video game, every smart app, every recommendation engine is built on this idea.
analogy: An if-statement is like a fork in the road — the sign (the condition) tells you which path to take, and you can only walk down one of them.
try_it: Change the `score` variable to different numbers — 90, 50, 30, 0 — and watch the output change. Then try changing `number` between positive and negative values. The same code, different results!
tips: The condition inside `if (...)` must be a Boolean — something that can be `true` or `false`.
You don't need `(...)` around the condition in XIOM — just write `if score >= 50 {` without parentheses.
Only ONE branch runs — the computer picks either the `if` block OR the `else` block, never both.
Indent the code inside `{ }` braces with two spaces — it makes your code much easier to read.
common_mistakes: Using `=` instead of `==` in the condition: `if score = 50` tries to put 50 into score, not check equality.
Putting a semicolon right after the condition: `if score >= 50; {` — no semicolon before the opening brace.
Forgetting the braces `{ }` — even if you only have one line, you still need the braces.
Writing `else` on its own without an `if` first — `else` always follows an `if` block.
